title: Λέων καὶ ἀλώπηξ καὶ ἔλαφος
titleEn: The Lion, the Fox, and the Deer
part: The Lion, the Fox, and the Deer (Chambry 199)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 199. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων νοσήσας ἔκειτο ἐν φάραγγι· τῇ προσφιλεῖ δὲ ἀλώπεκι, ᾗ προσωμίλει, εἶπεν· « Εἰ θέλεις ὑγιᾶναί με καὶ ζῆν, τὴν ἔλαφον τὴν μεγίστην, τὴν εἰς τὸν δρυμὸν οἰκοῦσαν, τοῖς γλυκέσι σου λόγοις ἐξαπατήσασα ἄγε εἰς ἐμὰς χεῖρας· ἐπιθυμῶ γὰρ αὐτῆς ἐγκάτων καὶ καρδίας. »
sentences.tr: Leōn nosēsas ekeito en pharangi· tēi prosphilei de alōpeki, hēi prosōmilei, eipen· « Ei theleis hygianai me kai zēn, tēn elaphon tēn megistēn, tēn eis ton drymon oikousan, tois glykesi sou logois exapatēsasa age eis emas cheiras· epithymō gar autēs enkatōn kai kardias. »
sentences.l: A lion, having fallen sick, lay in a ravine; and to the fox he was fond of, with whom he kept company, he said: « If you wish me to get well and to live, the largest deer, the one that dwells in the thicket, having deceived her with your sweet words, bring her into my hands; for I long for her innards and her heart. »
sentences.i: A lion fell sick and lay in a ravine; and to the fox he was fond of, whose company he kept, he said: « If you want me to recover and live, trick the biggest deer, the one that lives in the thicket, with your sweet words, and bring her into my hands; for I have a craving for her innards and her heart. »
sentences.n: This is one of the longest fables in the collection and one of the strangest — the language is late, the speeches are theatrical, and the whole of it turns on a pun kept back until the last line. ἔλαφος is feminine here throughout, so the deer is a doe, though the fable will give her horns and a mane. εἰς ἐμὰς χεῖρας: the beasts of this fable have hands, and will use them.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἀλώπηξ ἀπελθοῦσα εὗρε τὴν ἔλαφον σκιρτῶσαν ἐν ταῖς ὕλαις· προσπαίσασα δὲ αὐτῇ καὶ χαίρειν εἰποῦσα ἔφη· « Ἀγαθά σοι ἦλθον μηνῦσαι· οἶδας ὡς ὁ βασιλεὺς ἡμῶν λέων γείτων ἐστί μοι· νοσεῖ δὲ καὶ ἔστιν ἐγγὺς τοῦ θνῄσκειν.
sentences.tr: Hē de alōpēx apelthousa heure tēn elaphon skirtōsan en tais hylais· prospaisasa de autēi kai chairein eipousa ephē· « Agatha soi ēlthon mēnysai· oidas hōs ho basileus hēmōn leōn geitōn esti moi· nosei de kai estin engys tou thnēiskein.
sentences.l: And the fox, having gone off, found the deer frisking in the woods; and having sported with her and having bidden her rejoice, she said: « I have come to bring you good news. You know that our king the lion is a neighbour of mine; and he is sick and is near to dying.
sentences.i: The fox went off and found the deer frisking in the woods; she made playful approaches and greeted her, and said: « I have come with good news for you. You know that our king the lion is a neighbour of mine; and he is sick, and close to dying.
sentences.n: χαίρειν εἰπεῖν, 'to say rejoice', is the ordinary Greek for greeting someone — the word χαῖρε is the greeting itself. προσπαίζω is to sport or jest towards a person, the manner adopted before the business begins. The speech runs on unclosed here and for several sentences: Chambry opens the guillemets and does not shut them until the fox has finished.

sentences.t: Ἐβουλεύετο οὖν ποῖον τῶν θηρίων μετ’ αὐτὸν βασιλεύσει.
sentences.tr: Ebouleueto oun poion tōn thēriōn met’ auton basileusei.
sentences.l: So he was deliberating which of the beasts would be king after him.
sentences.n: An indirect question keeping the tense and mood of the original deliberation — the future indicative βασιλεύσει stands where English drops into 'would be'.

sentences.t: Ἔφη δὲ ὅτι σῦς μέν ἐστιν ἀγνώμων, ἄρκτος δὲ νωθρός, πάρδαλις δὲ θυμώδης, τίγρις ἀλαζών· ἡ ἔλαφος ἀξιωτάτη ἐστὶν εἰς βασιλείαν, ὅτι ὑψηλή ἐστι τὸ εἶδος, πολλὰ δὲ ἔτη ζῇ, τὸ κέρας αὐτῆς ὄφεσι φοβερόν.
sentences.tr: Ephē de hoti sys men estin agnōmōn, arktos de nōthros, pardalis de thymōdēs, tigris alazōn· hē elaphos axiōtatē estin eis basileian, hoti hypsēlē esti to eidos, polla de etē zēi, to keras autēs ophesi phoberon.
sentences.l: And he said that the boar is unfeeling, the bear sluggish, the leopard hot-tempered, the tiger a braggart; but the deer is most worthy for kingship, because she is lofty in form, and lives many years, and her horn is fearful to snakes.
sentences.i: And he said the boar is unfeeling, the bear sluggish, the leopard hot-tempered, the tiger a braggart; but the deer is the worthiest for kingship, since she is tall in build, lives many years, and her horn is a terror to snakes.
sentences.n: ὅτι introduces reported speech but the indicatives are kept exactly as spoken, so the survey reads like a transcript. τὸ εἶδος is an accusative of respect, 'in respect of form'. That burnt stag's horn drives away snakes was standard ancient natural history; the fox is flattering with textbook facts, which is what makes the flattery work.

sentences.t: Καὶ τί σοι τὰ πολλὰ λέγω ; ἐκυρώθης βασιλεύειν.
sentences.tr: Kai ti soi ta polla legō ; ekyrōthēs basileuein.
sentences.l: And why do I say the many things to you? You have been ratified to be king.
sentences.i: And why should I make a long story of it? You have been confirmed as king.
sentences.n: κυρόω is assembly language — the verb for a vote carried and made binding. The fox is not reporting an inclination but a decree, and the aorist passive makes it already done.

sentences.t: Τί μοι ἔσται πρώτῃ σοι εἰπούσῃ ;
sentences.tr: Ti moi estai prōtēi soi eipousēi ;
sentences.l: What will there be for me, the first to have told you?
sentences.i: And what do I get for being the first to bring you word?
sentences.n: πρώτῃ … εἰπούσῃ, both feminine dative, agree with μοι: the reward is claimed not for telling but for telling first.

sentences.t: Ἀλλ’ εὖξαί μοι σπευδούσῃ, μὴ πάλιν με ζητήσῃ· χρῄζει γάρ με σύμβουλον ἐν πᾶσιν.
sentences.tr: All’ euxai moi speudousēi, mē palin me zētēsēi· chrēizei gar me symboulon en pasin.
sentences.l: But wish me well as I hurry off, lest he look for me again; for he needs me as counsellor in everything.
sentences.n: εὔχομαι takes the dative of the person prayed for, and the participle σπευδούσῃ agrees with it. μή with the aorist subjunctive is the clause of apprehension: what she is afraid may happen. The fox slips in her own standing at court while pretending to be in a rush.

sentences.t: Εἰ δὲ ἐμοῦ τῆς γραὸς ἀκούσῃς, συμβουλεύω καὶ σὲ ἐλθεῖν καὶ προσμένειν τελευτῶντι αὐτῷ. »
sentences.tr: Ei de emou tēs graos akousēis, symbouleuō kai se elthein kai prosmenein teleutōnti autōi. »
sentences.l: But if you will listen to me, the old woman, I advise you too to come and to wait beside him as he dies. »
sentences.i: But if you will listen to me, an old woman, my advice is that you too should come and stay by him while he dies. »
sentences.n: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard. καὶ σέ is 'you too' — the fox is going back herself, and urges the deer to come as well. ἡ γραῦς, 'the old woman', is the fox's own word for herself — claiming the authority of years at the moment she is telling the biggest lie of the fable. τελευτῶντι αὐτῷ is a dative participle after προσμένειν: to stay by him in his dying.

sentences.t: Οὕτως εἶπεν ἡ ἀλώπηξ.
sentences.tr: Houtōs eipen hē alōpēx.
sentences.l: So spoke the fox.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ ὁ νοῦς ἐτυφώθη τοῖς λόγοις, καὶ ἦλθεν εἰς τὸ σπήλαιον μὴ γινώσκουσα τὸ μέλλον.
sentences.tr: Tēs de ho nous etyphōthē tois logois, kai ēlthen eis to spēlaion mē ginōskousa to mellon.
sentences.l: And her mind was befogged by the words, and she went to the cave, not knowing what was to come.
sentences.i: The words went to her head, and she came to the cave with no notion of what was waiting.
sentences.n: τυφόομαι is built on τῦφος, the smoke of a smouldering fire: to be smoked up, hence both clouded in judgement and swollen with conceit. Greek makes one word do what English needs two for; the moral at the end reaches for a kindred idea, though its picture there is muddied water rather than smoke.

sentences.t: Ὁ λέων δὲ ἐφορμήσας αὐτῇ ἐν σπουδῇ τὰ ὦτα μόνον τοῖς ὄνυξιν ἐσπάραξεν.
sentences.tr: Ho leōn de ephormēsas autēi en spoudēi ta ōta monon tois onyxin esparaxen.
sentences.l: But the lion, having rushed at her in his eagerness, tore only her ears with his claws.
sentences.i: But the lion sprang at her too eagerly, and got nothing but her ears, which he tore with his claws.
sentences.n: ἐφορμάω takes the dative of the quarry rushed at. ἐν σπουδῇ is the cause of the failure: a sick and starving lion cannot afford to hurry, and does.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ταχέως ἔσπευδεν ἐν ταῖς ὕλαις.
sentences.tr: Hē de tacheōs espeuden en tais hylais.
sentences.l: And she made off quickly among the woods.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ μὲν ἀλώπηξ τὰς χεῖρας ἐκρότησεν, ὅτι εἰς μάτην ἐκοπίασεν.
sentences.tr: Kai hē men alōpēx tas cheiras ekrotēsen, hoti eis matēn ekopiasen.
sentences.l: And the fox clapped her hands, because she had toiled to no purpose.
sentences.n: κροτεῖν τὰς χεῖρας is usually applause; here it is the clap of vexation, a gesture we should call throwing up one's hands. The fable has given the beasts hands from its first sentence and goes on using them.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λέων μέγα βρυχώμενος ἐστέναξεν· λιμὸς γὰρ αὐτὸν εἶχε καὶ λύπη· καὶ ἱκέτευε τὴν ἀλώπεκα ἐκ δευτέρου τι ποιῆσαι καὶ δόλῳ πάλιν ταύτην ἀγαγεῖν.
sentences.tr: Ho de leōn mega brychōmenos estenaxen· limos gar auton eiche kai lypē· kai hiketeue tēn alōpeka ek deuterou ti poiēsai kai dolōi palin tautēn agagein.
sentences.l: And the lion, roaring loudly, groaned; for hunger had hold of him, and grief; and he kept begging the fox to do something a second time and to bring her again by guile.
sentences.i: The lion gave a great roaring groan, for hunger had hold of him, and grief with it; and he begged the fox to try a second time and bring the deer back by a trick.
sentences.n: μέγα is an adverbial accusative, 'greatly, loudly'. ἐκ δευτέρου, 'from the second', is the ordinary phrase for a second attempt. ἱκετεύω is the verb of formal supplication — a king reduced to entreating his own minister.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ εἶπεν· « Χαλεπὸν καὶ δύσκολον ἐπιτάττεις ἐμοὶ πρᾶγμα, ἀλλ’ ὅμως ὑπουργήσω σοι ».
sentences.tr: Hē de eipen· « Chalepon kai dyskolon epitatteis emoi pragma, all’ homōs hypourgēsō soi ».
sentences.l: And she said: « A hard and disagreeable business you lay upon me, but all the same I will serve you ».
sentences.n: ἐπιτάττω is to impose an order from above, and the fox uses it to remind him he is commanding, not asking, even as she agrees. Chambry closes the quotation before the full stop here, as he prints it.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ ὡς ἰχνευτὴς κύων ἐπηκολούθει, πλέκουσα πανουργίας· ποιμένας δὲ ἐπηρώτα εἰ εἶδον ἔλαφον ᾑμαγμένην.
sentences.tr: Kai dē hōs ichneutēs kyōn epēkolouthei, plekousa panourgias· poimenas de epērōta ei eidon elaphon hēimagmenēn.
sentences.l: And so she followed the trail like a tracking hound, plaiting her knaveries; and she kept asking shepherds whether they had seen a deer covered with blood.
sentences.i: And so she went after her like a scent-hound, plaiting her tricks as she went, and asking the shepherds whether they had seen a deer covered in blood.
sentences.n: πλέκειν, 'to plait', is the old metaphor for constructing a plot, cousin to the ῥάπτειν, 'stitching', met elsewhere in these fables. ᾑμαγμένην is a perfect passive participle of αἱμάσσω: bloodied, and still so.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ ἔδειξαν ἐν τῇ ὕλῃ.
sentences.tr: Hoi de edeixan en tēi hylēi.
sentences.l: And they pointed her out in the wood.

sentences.t: Εὗρε δὲ αὐτὴν καταψυχομένην, καὶ ἔστη ἀναιδῶς.
sentences.tr: Heure de autēn katapsychomenēn, kai estē anaidōs.
sentences.l: And she found her cooling herself off, and stood there shamelessly.
sentences.n: καταψύχομαι is to cool down — the deer resting after her flight. ἔστη is the intransitive aorist of ἵστημι, 'took her stand'; ἀναιδῶς carries the fox's whole character in an adverb.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἔλαφος χολωθεῖσα καὶ φρίξασα τὴν χαίτην εἶπεν· « Ὦ κάθαρμα, ἀλλὰ οὐκέτι χειρώσῃ με· εἰ δὲ καὶ πλησιάσεις μοι, οὐ ζήσεις ἔτι.
sentences.tr: Hē de elaphos cholōtheisa kai phrixasa tēn chaitēn eipen· « Ō katharma, alla ouketi cheirōsēi me· ei de kai plēsiaseis moi, ou zēseis eti.
sentences.l: And the deer, enraged and having bristled up her mane, said: « You piece of filth, you will not master me again ; and if you so much as come near me, you will live no longer.
sentences.i: The deer, in a rage, her mane bristling, said: « You piece of filth, you will not get your hands on me again ; and if you so much as come near me, you will not live another moment.
sentences.n: κάθαρμα is the refuse swept off after a purification, and as abuse it is about as low as Greek goes. χαίτη, a mane, belongs to horses and lions rather than deer; this fable is not fastidious about its zoology.

sentences.t: Ἄλλους ἀλωπέκιζε τοὺς ἀπείρους, ἄλλους ποιεῖ βασιλεῖς καὶ ἐρέθιζε. »
sentences.tr: Allous alōpekize tous apeirous, allous poiei basileis kai erethize. »
sentences.l: Play the fox on others, on the inexperienced ; make others kings and provoke them. »
sentences.i: Go and play the fox on somebody else, on the green ones ; make somebody else king, and stir them up. »
sentences.n: ἀλωπεκίζω is a real Greek verb, 'to act the fox', and the deer throws the animal's own name at her as an insult. ἀλωπέκιζε and ἐρέθιζε are plain imperatives; ποιεῖ, as Chambry accents it, is the present indicative rather than the imperative ποίει, but standing between the other two it can only be meant as a third command. ἄλλους repeated at the head of the clauses is spoken fury, not composed rhetoric.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ εἶπεν· « Οὕτως ἄνανδρος εἶ καὶ δειλή ; οὕτως ἡμᾶς τοὺς φίλους ὑποπτεύεις ;
sentences.tr: Hē de eipen· « Houtōs anandros ei kai deilē ; houtōs hēmas tous philous hypopteueis ;
sentences.l: And she said: « Are you so unmanly and cowardly? Do you so suspect us, your friends?
sentences.n: ἄνανδρος is 'unmanly' whoever it is said of, and the deer is female — the Greek does not soften the word, and neither should the English. οὕτως at the head of both questions is the tone of injured astonishment.

sentences.t: Ὁ μὲν λέων τοῦ ὠτὸς κρατήσας ἤμελλε συμβουλεύειν καὶ ἐντολάς σοι δοῦναι περὶ τῆς τηλικαύτης βασιλείας ὡς ἀποθνῄσκων· σὺ δὲ οὐδὲ κνίσμα χειρὸς ἀρρώστου ὑπέστης.
sentences.tr: Ho men leōn tou ōtos kratēsas ēmelle symbouleuein kai entolas soi dounai peri tēs tēlikautēs basileias hōs apothnēiskōn· sy de oude knisma cheiros arrōstou hypestēs.
sentences.l: The lion, taking hold of your ear, was going to counsel you and to give you instructions about so great a kingship, as a dying man does; but you did not endure even the scratch of a sick hand.
sentences.i: The lion took you by the ear meaning to advise you and give you his instructions about a kingship of that size, as a dying man does; and you would not put up with so much as a scratch from a sick hand.
sentences.n: κρατέω takes the genitive of what is grasped. ὡς ἀποθνῄσκων gives the lion's own view of himself — 'seeing that he is dying'. The impudence of the speech is that it re-describes the mauling as a private word in the ear, and dares the deer to have taken offence at it.

sentences.t: Καὶ νῦν ὑπὲρ σὲ πλεῖον ἐκεῖνος θυμοῦται, καὶ βασιλέα τὸν λύκον θέλει ποιῆσαι· οἴμοι, πονηρὸν δεσπότην.
sentences.tr: Kai nyn hyper se pleion ekeinos thymoutai, kai basilea ton lykon thelei poiēsai· oimoi, ponēron despotēn.
sentences.l: And now he is the more enraged over you, and wants to make the wolf king — alas, a wicked master.
sentences.i: And now he is angrier than ever on your account, and means to make the wolf king — a bad master, alas for us.
sentences.n: ὑπὲρ σέ with the accusative where the genitive would be expected, 'over you, on your account'; the construction is loose, as much of this fable's Greek is. πονηρὸν δεσπότην is an accusative of exclamation, standing outside the sentence's grammar altogether.

sentences.t: Ἀλλ’ ἐλθὲ καὶ μηδὲν πτοηθῇς καὶ γενοῦ ὡς πρόβατον.
sentences.tr: All’ elthe kai mēden ptoēthēis kai genou hōs probaton.
sentences.l: But come, and do not be frightened at all, and become like a sheep.
sentences.n: μηδέν is adverbial, 'not in the least'; μή with the aorist subjunctive is the regular way to forbid a single act. ὡς πρόβατον is meant as reassurance and is the plainest possible statement of what is about to happen to her.

sentences.t: Ὄμνυμι γάρ σοι εἰς τὰ φύλλα πάντα καὶ πηγὰς μηδὲν κακὸν παθεῖν παρὰ τοῦ λέοντος· ἐγὼ δὲ μόνῃ σοι δουλεύσω. »
sentences.tr: Omnymi gar soi eis ta phylla panta kai pēgas mēden kakon pathein para tou leontos· egō de monēi soi douleusō. »
sentences.l: For I swear to you by all the leaves and springs that you will suffer no harm from the lion; and I will be a servant to you alone. »
sentences.i: For I swear to you by every leaf and spring that you will come to no harm from the lion; and I will serve you and no one else. »
sentences.n: ὄμνυμι with εἰς and the accusative is a late way of naming what one swears by; the classical construction uses the plain accusative or a preposition of a different sort. What the fox swears by is the woods themselves — the only holy things a deer would recognise.

sentences.t: Οὕτως ἀπατήσασα τὴν δειλαίαν ἔπεισε δεύτερον ἐλθεῖν.
sentences.tr: Houtōs apatēsasa tēn deilaian epeise deuteron elthein.
sentences.l: Thus having deceived the wretched creature she persuaded her to come a second time.

sentences.t: Ἐπεὶ δὲ εἰς τὸ σπήλαιον εἰσῆλθεν, ὁ μὲν λέων δεῖπνον εἶχε, πάντα τὰ ὀστᾶ καὶ μυελοὺς καὶ ἔγκατα αὐτῆς καταπίνων.
sentences.tr: Epei de eis to spēlaion eisēlthen, ho men leōn deipnon eiche, panta ta osta kai myelous kai enkata autēs katapinōn.
sentences.l: And when she had gone into the cave, the lion had his dinner, swallowing down all her bones and marrow and innards.
sentences.n: δεῖπνον εἶχε is flatly domestic — 'he had dinner' — and the participle that follows spells out what dinner was. The fable does not look away, and the translation does not either.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἀλώπηξ εἱστήκει ὁρῶσα· καρδίαν δὲ ἐκπεσοῦσαν ἁρπάζει λαθραίως, τοῦ κόπου κέρδος ταύτην φαγοῦσα.
sentences.tr: Hē de alōpēx heistēkei horōsa· kardian de ekpesousan harpazei lathraiōs, tou kopou kerdos tautēn phagousa.
sentences.l: And the fox stood looking on; and the heart, having fallen out, she snatches secretly, eating it as the profit of her labour.
sentences.i: The fox stood watching; and when the heart fell out she snatched it up on the sly and ate it, the wages of her work.
sentences.n: εἱστήκει is a pluperfect of ἵστημι doing the work of an imperfect: she had taken her stand and was standing. ἁρπάζει is a historic present dropped in among the past tenses, the one quick movement in a still scene. τοῦ κόπου κέρδος stands in apposition to ταύτην — the heart is the fee.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λέων ἅπαντα ἐρευνήσας μόνην καρδίαν ἐπεζήτει.
sentences.tr: Ho de leōn hapanta ereunēsas monēn kardian epezētei.
sentences.l: And the lion, having searched everything, kept looking for the heart alone.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ δὲ μηκόθεν σταθεῖσα ἔφη· « Αὕτη ἀληθῶς καρδίαν οὐκ εἶχεν· μὴ ἔτι ζήτει· ποίαν γὰρ καρδίαν αὕτη εἶχεν, ἥτις δὶς εἰς οἶκον καὶ χεῖρας λέοντος εἰσῆλθεν. »
sentences.tr: Alōpēx de mēkothen statheisa ephē· « Hautē alēthōs kardian ouk eichen· mē eti zētei· poian gar kardian hautē eichen, hētis dis eis oikon kai cheiras leontos eisēlthen. »
sentences.l: And the fox, having taken her stand far off, said: « This one truly had no heart. Look no longer; for what sort of heart did she have, who twice went into the house and the hands of a lion. »
sentences.i: The fox took her stand well away and said: « She truly had no heart. Stop looking. What sort of heart could she have had, who walked twice into a lion's house and a lion's hands. »
sentences.n: The whole fable has been waiting for this: καρδία is the organ the lion is hunting for and also the seat of sense and courage, so 'she had no heart' is at once the fox's alibi and her verdict. Chambry prints the last clause with a full stop, not a question mark — an exclamation in the shape of a question. μηκόθεν, 'from afar', is a late by-form of μακρόθεν, and the fox is careful to stand where the lion cannot reach.

sentences.t: Ὅτι ὁ τῆς φιλοδοξίας ἔρως τὸν ἀνθρώπινον νοῦν ἐπιθολοῖ καὶ τὰς τῶν κινδύνων συμφορὰς οὐ κατανοεῖ.
sentences.tr: Hoti ho tēs philodoxias erōs ton anthrōpinon noun epitholoi kai tas tōn kindynōn symphoras ou katanoei.
sentences.l: That the love of glory muddies the human mind and does not perceive the calamities that come of dangers.
sentences.i: The story shows that the love of glory muddies the human mind and takes no notice of the disasters that danger brings.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ἐπιθολόω is to stir mud through clear water — a different picture from the ἐτυφώθη, 'was smoked up', of the deer's mind earlier, but the same charge of a clouded mind. As printed, the subject of οὐ κατανοεῖ is still ἔρως, though it is the clouded mind that fails to see — the Greek runs the two together rather than changing subject.
